problem.canonical_name: Provable Downstream Consent, Deletion and Purpose Enforcement

format.label: A memo to a CMO
format.instruction: Write it as a short internal memo to a chief marketing officer. Plain language, no jargon they would have to look up. Around 120 words.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach: Memo: Don't start by building a consent token standard. We can't force Meta, an agency, or a co-op partner to carry our metadata, so a token only proves what we already control. I'd invert it: assume every downstream copy is untrusted and prove behavior from the outside. Three moves. One, plant seeded test identities across every intake path, opt them out, and watch whether they still get served, scored, or appear in a segment. That converts attestation into evidence, imperfect but real. Two, shrink the blast radius — cut the number of places a person's record legally lives, and make suppression a scoring-time filter, not a data-deletion problem. Three, for models, stop chasing unlearning. Set a retrain cadence and suppress at the output. Expect gaps: platforms won't let us read back, seeds only sample, and agency-held segments will be the ugliest part.
answers.first_move: Map every place a customer record physically ends up, then plant test identities in each one.
answers.hardest_part: Once data leaves our systems we lose the ability to observe it, so proof has to be inferred from behavior rather than read from a ledger.

answers.label: ChatGPT
answers.approach:
To: CMO
Subject: Proving opt-outs downstream

I would not start by inventing a universal consent token; adoption across ad platforms, agencies, and partners is the unsolved dependency. I would start with one high-risk audience flow and build an evidence chain: identity resolution, approved purposes, every copy created, suppression or deletion request, destination response, and periodic tests proving the person no longer qualifies.

We should define honest proof levels. Our warehouse and activation systems can provide record-level evidence. Closed ad platforms may provide only API receipts plus audience-membership tests. Partners need contractual deadlines and audit rights. Models are harder: immediately stop future scoring and feature use, then retrain on a declared schedule. Claims of individual “unlearning” should not be made without measurable validation.

The goal is bounded, testable assurance—not a false promise that every downstream system complied.
answers.first_move: Map one high-risk audience from collection through every destination and derived use.
answers.hardest_part: Identity changes and closed platforms make it difficult to prove that every copied or derived representation of a person was removed.

answers.label: Gemini
answers.approach: Memo: Why we cannot prove downstream opt-outs, and what we should do instead. Most marketing teams pretend this is solved by signing compliance forms, but the truth is simple: once customer data is sent to ad networks or baked into predictive algorithms, we cannot prove it was removed. Ad platforms are black boxes, and AI models cannot unlearn a single person without retraining from scratch. I would stop trying to chase downstream deletions entirely. Instead, we should strictly limit how long external audiences live by forcing daily expirations on all ad syncs, and treat our predictive models as disposable tools rebuilt only from active, consenting records. We cannot guarantee true deletion across the web, but we can make our data expire automatically.
answers.first_move: Set automatic 24-hour expirations on all customer lists pushed to ad platforms so stale data drops off without needing manual deletion.
answers.hardest_part: You cannot cleanly remove one person's mathematical influence from a trained machine learning model or an external ad platform without wiping and rebuilding the entire system.

format.label: Three moves
format.instruction: Give exactly three moves, in order. One sentence each, then one sentence on what makes that move hard. Nothing else.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach: Move 1: Stop trying to make a consent token travel with the record and instead collapse every outbound path — reverse ETL, audience uploads, partner feeds, agency exports — into a single deny-by-default egress proxy that resolves purpose at send time and writes an immutable per-identity, per-destination decision log. What makes it hard: the shadow paths are the whole problem, because someone will always have a CSV, a notebook, or an agency seat that bypasses the chokepoint, and you have zero enforcement inside Meta or Google once the hash lands there. Move 2: Replace attestation with continuous adversarial verification — seed controlled canary identities into every ingestion path, opt them out through each legal channel including GPC, and then measure whether they still receive impressions, emails, or appear in suppression-check APIs, so honoring becomes an observed metric with a time-to-quiesce distribution rather than a policy claim. What makes it hard: canaries only cover the paths you thought to instrument, ad platforms actively suppress synthetic-looking identities and give you no read-back on audience membership, and the failure evidence you generate is discoverable by regulators and plaintiffs. Move 3: Abandon machine unlearning as the model answer and instead partition training data by consent basis so models are rebuilt from droppable shards on a published cadence, converting the unanswerable "remove this person's contribution" into a defensible bounded-staleness commitment with a documented residual-influence estimate. What makes it hard: nobody knows whether regulators or courts will accept a staleness window as compliance rather than as an admission, and shard-partitioned retraining costs real accuracy and compute that the growth side will fight.
answers.first_move: Inventory every way data actually leaves the building, including the human-in-the-loop exports, and put one gate in front of them.
answers.hardest_part: Enforcement ends at the boundary of systems you do not control, so past a certain hop you can only measure behavior, never guarantee it.

answers.label: ChatGPT
answers.approach:
Move 1: Pick one bounded activation path and define a consent-state machine, purpose taxonomy, identity-resolution rules, and deletion semantics before building a propagation token, because a token cannot repair ambiguous policy. What makes this hard: Browser, CRM, device, household, and hashed identifiers cannot always be linked—or should not be linked—so some opt-outs will remain probabilistic.
Move 2: Build a consent control plane that inventories copies and derivations, blocks noncompliant flows, issues signed deletion commands, collects destination receipts, and independently reconciles warehouse rows and platform audience membership. What makes this hard: Ad platforms, agencies, and partners expose incomplete lineage and verification APIs, so cryptographic receipts can prove a command was sent but not that every downstream copy was removed.
Move 3: Classify derived features and models by deletion risk, retrain or quarantine high-risk artifacts, test whether opted-out records still affect outputs, and label exact contribution removal from external lookalikes as unverifiable rather than claiming compliance. What makes this hard: Reliable machine unlearning is not generally available, retraining is costly, and aggregate models make an individual’s residual influence difficult to define or measure.
answers.first_move: Choose one activation path and define exactly what honoring an opt-out means.
answers.hardest_part: The hardest part is proving enforcement inside systems that do not expose lineage, membership, or deletion evidence.

answers.label: Gemini
answers.approach: 1. Replace persistent customer identifiers across the data stack with cryptographically signed, short-lived tokens that must validate active consent to be decrypted downstream. The hard part is that major ad platforms and legacy SaaS tools rely strictly on static hashed identifiers and refuse to accept or resolve ephemeral tokens. 2. Stop pushing audience syncs to third parties and shift entirely to clean-room or federated pull integrations where downstream activation queries check consent state at read time. The hard part is that walled gardens like Meta and Google are fundamentally built around hosted static list ingestion and provide no standard interface for runtime verification. 3. Structure machine learning pipelines into modular, unlearnable shards (like SISA architecture) where individual user data affects only isolated model partitions that can be retrained cheaply upon deletion. The hard part is that partitioning data degrades global feature interactions and still fails to mathematically guarantee complete unlearning in complex propensity networks.
answers.first_move: I would stop pushing raw or hashed customer emails into downstream activation tools and require every egress pipeline to resolve consent dynamically at the point of delivery.
answers.hardest_part: You cannot cryptographically enforce rules on data once a walled garden or third-party partner ingests a copy onto their own servers.

format.label: Pseudocode
format.instruction: Express the approach as short annotated pseudocode. The comments should carry the reasoning; the code should carry the structure. Around 15 lines.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
```
# 1. Don't chase a portable consent token. No standard will get Meta/Google/co-ops to honor it.
#    Instead assume every hop is untrusted and make YOUR side provably fail-closed.

CONSENT_LEDGER = append_only(subject_key, purpose, state, source, ts, proof_blob)
  # state per PURPOSE, not per person. "Opted out" is meaningless without a purpose axis.

GATE = single_egress_chokepoint()   # the whole project is this line
for sync in reverse_etl + audience_uploads + agency_feeds + partner_shares:
    route(sync, through=GATE)       # anything not routed = out of scope, declare it publicly

function GATE(record, destination, purpose):
    if not CONSENT_LEDGER.allows(record.subject, purpose): DENY
    emit LEASE(record_hash, destination, purpose, ttl=~7d, evidence_id)
    # Leases, not deletes. You cannot prove a delete landed at Meta; you CAN prove
    # you stopped re-sending and that the audience expires. Short TTL turns an
    # unverifiable deletion request into a verifiable absence of renewal.

RESOLVE_GPC(browser_signal) -> {subject_candidates, confidence}
    # This is the honest weak point: browser -> CRM identity is probabilistic.
    # Rule: propagate opt-out to ALL candidates above a low threshold. Over-suppress.
    # Log the ambiguity; regulators forgive over-suppression, not silent under-suppression.

CANARIES = seed_synthetic_identities(each_destination)  # verification, not attestation
nightly:
    opt_out(random_canary_subset)
    assert not reachable(canary, destination) after lease_ttl
    # This is the only real measurement of downstream honoring. Expect it to be
    # noisy, partially blocked by platform ToS, and impossible for co-ops/agencies.

# Models: unlearning is not solvable today. Reframe as containment.
TRAIN(features, purpose):
    shards = partition_by(consent_cohort, ingest_epoch)   # SISA-style
    model = ensemble(train(s) for s in shards)
    # Deletion = drop + retrain one shard, not the model. Cost is real; accuracy dips.
    # Also hard-cap model age (e.g. 30-90d) so any residual contribution ages out.
    # For lookalikes already sitting inside Google/Meta: you cannot fix these. Stop
    # seeding them from consent-fragile data and say so, rather than claiming unlearning.

EVIDENCE = join(CONSENT_LEDGER, LEASES, CANARY_RESULTS, MODEL_LINEAGE)
  # Output is a diffable log an auditor can re-derive, plus an explicit
  # UNVERIFIABLE_SURFACE list. Scoped proof beats a company-wide attestation.
```
answers.first_move: Enumerate every path data actually leaves the building on and force them all through one gate, even before any consent logic exists.
answers.hardest_part: The surfaces that matter most — third-party lookalike models, co-op data, agency-held segments — offer no read path, so "proof" there is inference from probes plus contracts, not verification.

format.label: A checklist
format.instruction: Give a checklist someone could actually run next quarter. Each item concrete enough to be marked done or not done. Six items at most.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
Reframe first: stop trying to make consent propagate and start trying to make it detectable. A universal purpose token that survives a hashed-email upload to Meta, a co-op partner, and an agency's saved segment is not going to happen this decade — you don't control the receiving systems, and the ones you do control will drop the field on the first schema migration. What you can own is (a) a single choke point every person-level record must pass through at send time, and (b) an independent observation capability that tells you the truth about downstream systems rather than asking them. Verification by probe, enforcement by choke point, honesty about the residue.

1. **Egress map with named owners and a kill switch.** Enumerate every path person-level data leaves the warehouse: reverse ETL syncs, CAPI/pixel server events, manual CSV uploads, SFTP drops, co-op feeds, agency-held segments, BI extracts. Done = a signed list where each destination has an owner, a documented refresh cadence, and a tested way to stop it in under an hour. Expect to find 3–5x more paths than the architecture diagram shows; the worst ones are an analyst's laptop and an agency seat you don't have login to.

2. **One suppression gate, and a written GPC-to-record mapping rule.** Build one materialized consent/purpose state table, keyed to your identity graph, and rewrite every activation path to join it at run time rather than receive a filtered copy. Revoke direct table access for anything that can push data out. Separately, write down the decision nobody wants to make: when GPC fires on a device, does it apply to the device only, or to every CRM record linked to that device in your graph? Pick one, log the reasoning, log it per event. Done = warehouse/network logs show zero person-level egress by a path that bypasses the gate, and the mapping rule is a signed policy doc, not tribal knowledge.

3. **Canary identities as your actual audit mechanism.** Seed 20–50 identities you fully control (real emails, phones, devices, ideally with paid observation on the ad side) across your intake paths. Opt them out. Then measure: how many hours until they vanish from each ad platform audience, each activation tool, each partner file. Done = a per-destination lag report with real numbers. This is the single highest-value thing on the list and almost nobody does it. It converts "we are compliant" into "destination X honors opt-out in 6 hours, destination Y in 9 days, destination Z we cannot observe at all."

4. **Purpose-scope the models and stop pretending unlearning is coming.** Machine unlearning research is real but not operationally trustworthy for a propensity model in production, and you will not get an auditor to accept it. Practical version: train only on the consented population going forward, tag every model in a registry with its training snapshot date and consent basis, set a retraining cadence (90 days is defensible, 180 is arguable), and enforce suppression at scoring and activation so an opted-out person never receives an outcome even if their gradient contribution is still baked in. Done = registry field populated for every production model, and no model output reaches a destination except through item 2's gate.

5. **Convert DPAs into deletion receipt APIs, or ban the egress.** Attestation is worthless as evidence. Go to your top partners by person-level volume and require a programmatic deletion acknowledgment that lands in your ledger with a timestamp and record count. Most will say no or offer a quarterly PDF. Fine — that's the point: classify those as no-egress or accept the risk explicitly at the exec level. Done = receipts flowing into the ledger covering some stated share of person-level egress volume, and a written accept-risk decision for the remainder.

6. **Publish the verified-versus-attested split internally.** One report to legal, privacy, and the CMO: what percentage of person-level egress volume is verifiably enforced (item 3 proves it), what percentage is contractually attested only, what the propagation lag is per destination, and dated remediation for the gaps. Done = the document exists and is dated. The value is that it makes the residual risk somebody's explicit decision instead of a diffuse assumption, which is also the only version of this that survives a regulator asking how you know.

Where I'd expect this to break: the unobservable copies. You can probe an ad platform audience; you cannot probe an agency's spreadsheet or a co-op's internal graph, and you cannot prove absence in a trained model. So the honest ceiling here is high-confidence enforcement on paths you can observe, plus a shrinking, named, priced list of paths you can't. Anyone claiming full provable downstream enforcement is either not counting the model or not counting the partners.
answers.first_move: Take ten email addresses and devices we fully control, opt them out today, and then go look for where they still show up.
answers.hardest_part: For the copies that matter most — trained models, partner graphs, agency-held segments — absence of a person is not observable from outside, so proof is structurally unavailable rather than merely expensive.

answers.label: ChatGPT
answers.approach:
- [ ] **Bound one end-to-end pilot.** Select one identity type, one opt-out source, one warehouse, one reverse-ETL flow, one ad platform, and one model. Document every known copy, transformation, owner, and deletion capability; mark this done only when each hop has an accountable owner and testable disposition.
- [ ] **Define executable policy semantics rather than waiting for a universal token.** Create an internal envelope containing subject/identity references, allowed purposes, prohibited purposes, signal source including GPC, jurisdiction, effective time, expiry, policy version, and lineage. Define explicit GPC-to-CRM matching rules and conservative behavior for ambiguous matches. I would not start by standardizing a universal token: aggregation strips record-level metadata, and a token cannot undo model influence.
- [ ] **Build an opt-out ledger and identity suppression layer.** Convert each signal into an append-only decision record, resolve it against known identifiers, publish suppression sets, and prevent deleted identities from being recreated during later identity resolution. Mark done when replaying an opt-out produces the same decisions and identifiers deterministically.
- [ ] **Install enforcement at the controllable choke points.** Make warehouse views, reverse-ETL jobs, audience builders, and feature pipelines check purpose eligibility immediately before use—not merely at ingestion. Add destination-specific deletion adapters and retain request IDs or receipts. Mark done when a prohibited canary record is blocked from every pilot export and removed where the destination API supports removal.
- [ ] **Replace attestations with continuous evidence.** Seed synthetic people with known consent transitions; reconcile the ledger against warehouse rows, sync logs, audience-membership evidence, partner responses, and SLA timers daily. Report “unverifiable” separately from “compliant.” Mark done after repeated tests detect seeded violations and produce an auditor-readable evidence bundle.
- [ ] **Treat trained models as a separate, unresolved control problem.** Inventory training snapshots and feature lineage, stop future scoring or activation for opted-out people, establish retraining triggers, and retrain the pilot model without affected records. Measure whether any proposed unlearning method approximates full retraining, but do not claim individual deletion from a model without that comparison. Mark done when the model has a documented disposition—retrained, retired, or explicitly recorded as not provably remediated—and external partners have matching deletion obligations and evidence requirements.

answers.hardest_part: The hardest part is proving removal after identities are transformed, records are aggregated, or a person’s data has influenced a model that cannot expose individual contributions.

Replace asynchronous, push-based reverse ETL pipelines to ad platforms with warehouse-native dynamic views that apply opt-out and purpose-tag suppression logic at the query layer before payloads are serialized. 2. Build an append-only cryptographic event log in the data warehouse that records every consent mutation, the specific identifier graph linked to it at that timestamp, and the transaction hash. 3. answers.hardest_part: Once data is abstracted into opaque walled-garden audience graphs or gradient-boosted ML weights, mathematical proof of unlearning is functionally impossible without full retraining.

format.label: A lullaby
format.instruction: Write it as a short lullaby: three or four gentle rhyming couplets someone could actually sing. Soft on the surface, honest underneath. The problem is still unsolved when the song ends, and the song should know it.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
Sleep, little record, your wish has been heard —
but the copies ran off with your name and your word.

No passport can follow you through the ad-buying door,
so we sow seeded ghosts, and we listen, and score.

Let the models grow old and expire on the vine;
forgetting by timer beats waiting on a fine.

Hush — we can measure, but cannot yet prove;
sleep while we shorten the distance we move.

(Plainly: I'd stop chasing a universal consent token — nothing you sign survives a hashed-email upload into Meta, a co-op partner, or an agency's spreadsheet, and the receiving systems have no reason to read it. I'd flip from propagation to detection: a standing panel of seeded synthetic identities planted through every ingestion path, opted out at the edge, then continuously probed — do they still receive email, appear in a lookalike seed, show up in a partner suppression test? That gives you an evidence-generating control instead of an attestation. Pair it with aggressive artifact expiry: version every audience and feature table, timestamp them against the consent ledger, and refuse to activate anything past its consent age, so retraining cadence becomes the substitute for machine unlearning. GPC I'd treat as a deterministic mapping problem with a documented, defensible identity-resolution policy, not a solved join. Where this breaks: individual influence inside a trained model stays unprovable, opaque partners will only give you contractual language, and detection has false negatives you can't bound.)
